newsitem.title: UK: Rallies in metals, wheat dominate commodities.
newsitem.headline: Rallies in metals, wheat dominate commodities.

text.p: Metals markets took the lead in commodities trading on Wednesday as copper, gold and silver mounted brisk rallies, although they were eventually reined in by bouts of speculator selling.
Wheat prices in Chicago also pushed higher after a recent slide on signs the European Union may be scaling back the amount of subsidy it offers for wheat exports.
European Commission Director-General David Roberts said the EU will have to use caution in its grain export subsidy policy for the rest of 1996-97 (July-June) due to budgetary problems.
Talk that Egypt by the weekend would be in for 250,000 to 300,000 tonnes of wheat and that the business may go to the United States was also supportive, the traders said.
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said he expected wheat prices to rebound as supplies became tighter.

"I think that's already begun to happen...It did seem to fall extremely rapidly in a very short period of time. I'm concerned about that. I do believe those markets will come back," Glickman said at a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit.
Copper rallied to fresh 2-1/2 month highs, peaking at $2,083 per tonne on speculative buying and expectations of stock falls.
But it then drifted lower and remained below early peaks on the London Metal Exchange (LME).
"Copper has been volatile in fairly good volume. Although off its highs it seems to be establishing a new higher range," an LME floor trader said.
But there was some stiff resistance and selling above $2,075 with the market also unsettled by an analysts' report that there may be substantial hidden stocks in the Netherlands.
In the precious metals markets, gold and silver staged a serious attempt to push higher in the third positive day in a row after a recent break-out from a weeks-old downtrend.
Gold closed more than $2.00 higher an ounce compared to Tuesday, but hefty selling appeared to cap gold's rise around $384.00. Silver struggled with resistance at $4.92 an ounce.
"If there are any longer term speculators around still expecting a fall, then $385.00 is likely to be where they would come and cover," a dealer said.
Oil prices continued a roller coaster ride on Wednesday as losses suffered Tuesday were erased but the recovery failed to convince traders that any clear direction had emerged.

At 1745 GMT benchmark December Brent crude oil futures on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) were around $23.25 per barrel. Prices are firm on concern about the level of heating oil stocks in Europe and the United States.
Cocoa was weaker in London, down nine stg at 916 stg, after slipping to a fresh seven-month low, and coffee ended down after choppy trading.
